opus-5.5.text:
I think what worries me most is that fundraising has become a kind of product in itself. In physical AI right now, a lot of teams are optimizing for the next round rather than for the robot actually working in a real environment. You see very polished demo videos: a humanoid folding laundry, picking up a cup. These are often teleoperated, or heavily curated from many attempts, and they get used as the main signal to investors. Then the valuation jumps, and the company has to justify that valuation with an even more impressive demo six months later. It becomes a cycle that's disconnected from the hard, boring work of reliability.

In physical systems, the gap between "it worked once on camera" and "it works 99.9% of the time in a customer's factory or home" is enormous. That last stretch is where most of the real engineering lives: hardware durability, safety, data collection at scale, failure recovery, cost. None of it looks exciting in a pitch deck. So when capital floods in based on demos, it tends to reward the wrong behaviors.

The second concern is talent and resource concentration. When a few companies raise huge rounds at very high valuations, they pull in engineers, compute, and supply chain attention, but the underlying problems, like generalizable manipulation or good world models for contact-rich tasks, aren't solved just by spending more. You can't brute-force the data problem in robotics the same way you could scrape the internet for language models. So there's a risk that lots of money gets burned without proportional progress, and then the whole sector gets punished when sentiment turns.

And that's the third thing: I worry about a bubble-and-winter dynamic. If expectations are set too high, too early, and the products don't arrive on schedule, investors pull back broadly, including from teams doing solid, patient work. We've seen this before with autonomous driving. Those of us who believe physical AI is a long-term transformation should care about keeping expectations honest, because overpromising today makes it harder to fund the real progress tomorrow.

So my view is that money is necessary, but it should follow evidence of real deployment, real customers, real learning loops, not just spectacle.

r001.rationale: The candidate says teams optimize for the next round, use polished demos as the main signal to investors, and are then pressured to produce even more impressive demos. This clearly describes investor-facing promotion being rewarded through continual fundraising.

fable-5.1.text:
What worries me is that the industry has started to treat the financing round itself as the product. You look at the headlines coming out of embodied AI over the past two years, and the story is almost always about valuation, not about what the robot can actually do in a factory or a warehouse on a Tuesday afternoon when nobody from the demo team is standing nearby.

I understand why it happens. Hardware is expensive, the timelines are long, and if you don't raise you don't survive. But when the capital arrives before the technical problems are solved, it changes the incentives inside the company. Teams start optimizing for the next milestone that investors can recognize, which usually means a video, a partnership announcement, a new form factor. Those things are legible. Reliability over ten thousand hours is not legible. Unit economics that actually work at scale are not legible. So the hard, boring work gets pushed down the priority list.

The second thing that concerns me is that the money is converging on a narrow set of narratives. Humanoids are the obvious example. Everyone is chasing the general-purpose humanoid because that's the story that commands the biggest number. Meanwhile there are a lot of unglamorous problems in logistics, agriculture, and manufacturing where a simpler machine with better data and a clear buyer could be generating revenue today. The fundraising frenzy crowds those out, because a company solving a specific problem looks small next to a company promising to replace human labor.

And the third concern is what happens when the cycle turns. We've seen this before in autonomous driving. Enormous valuations, enormous confidence, and then a long and painful period where capital dried up and a lot of real engineering talent got scattered. If physical AI goes through the same thing, the damage isn't just to investors. It sets back the field, because the people who actually understand how to make these systems work end up leaving.

So I'm not against raising money. I'm against raising money becoming the scoreboard. The scoreboard should be deployments, uptime, and whether a customer renews. If a company can talk about those numbers with the same enthusiasm it talks about its Series B, that's when I start paying attention.

r001.rationale: The response says teams optimize for investor-recognizable milestones such as videos and partnership announcements, making those promotional activities more rewarded than less visible engineering work.

astra-6.text:
What concerns me is when fundraising becomes the measure of progress. In physical AI, the real test is whether a system can do useful work reliably, safely, and at a cost a customer can justify. A compelling demo and a large funding round don’t necessarily tell you that.

Of course, this work needs capital. Hardware, testing, and deployment are expensive. But if the next round becomes the main objective, teams can end up optimizing for what looks impressive to investors rather than learning from actual use. I’d like to hear more about what happens after the demo: how often does the system fail, how much human intervention does it need, and does the customer keep using it?

r001.rationale: It says that when the next funding round becomes the main objective, teams optimize for what impresses investors, making investor-facing promotion a rewarded activity.

sol-6.1.text:
What concerns me is when fundraising becomes the measure of progress. In physical AI, an impressive demo and a large funding round don’t necessarily mean a system can work reliably in the real world. You still have to solve safety, cost, maintenance, and all the unexpected situations that arise outside a controlled environment.

Capital is necessary, but it should support that work. If companies spend more energy telling a compelling story to investors than understanding customers’ needs, we risk building expectations faster than we build useful products. I’d rather see the industry judged by what gets deployed, how consistently it works, and whether customers actually benefit.

r001.rationale: The response says fundraising can become a measure of progress and that companies may spend more energy telling investors a compelling story. It does not clearly explain that continually pursuing fundraising rewards investor-facing promotion as a team activity.
